item.research_question: How does varying the mechanical alloying milling time affect the microstructural evolution, phase composition, contamination levels, and mechanical properties of the Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) produced via powder metallurgy?
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying in a Fritsch Pulverisette 6 planetary ball mill under high-purity argon (99.9999%) using hardened steel balls (AISI 52100, 15 mm diameter) at 250 RPM with a 10:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio; subsequent consolidation via spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C, 50 MPa uniaxial pressure, 100 °C·min⁻¹ heating rate, and 15 min dwell time.
item.test_conditions: Milling times of 0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 hours; sintering of powders milled for 3, 10, 30, and 50 hours; microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness (0.2 kgf load), nanoindentation (100 mN max load), and ultrasound methods.
key_findings: Carbide formation (ZrC) was detected in sintered bulks as early as after 3 hours of powder milling.
Oxides (TiO2) were observed in bulks prepared from powders milled for 30 hours or longer.
The bulk produced from 50 h milled powders exhibited the highest hardness of 675.7 ± 9.8 HV0.2.
The bulk produced from 3 h milled powders exhibited the lowest hardness of 592.9 ± 21.0 HV0.2.
The elastic modulus increased from 134.7 GPa (3 h) to 138.7 GPa (50 h).
Iron contamination in the matrix increased from undetectable levels to 1.8 at.% (30 h) and 2.2 at.% (50 h).
Average grain size of the BCC matrix decreased from 33.8 µm (3 h) to 25.2 µm (50 h).
10 hours of milling was found sufficient to achieve a virtually fully homogeneously alloyed state with a dominant BCC phase.
item.mechanism: Longer milling times induce severe plastic deformation, refining powder particle size and increasing lattice strain, which leads to more refined microstructures and higher hardness in the sintered bulks. However, prolonged milling causes wear of the carbon steel milling media, introducing carbon and oxygen that form ZrC carbides and TiO2 oxides during sintering, which contribute to strengthening but also increase contamination.
item.limitations: The study notes that the formation of oxides and carbides is nearly unavoidable in powder metallurgy even with controlled atmospheres due to equipment wear, and that longer milling times inevitably increase contamination levels (Fe, C, O), which may negatively affect ductility.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the formation of oxides/carbides could be exploited to explore the oxide dispersed strengthening (ODS) effect, and that the process parameters should be optimized to balance microstructural refinement with minimal contamination.
quotes: Milling time seems to play a significant role in the contamination level of the sintered materials.
Ten hours of milling seems sufficient for achieving an optimal equilibrium between microstructural homogeneity and refinement, high hardness and minimal contamination.
The sintered alloy corresponding to 50 h of mechanical alloying exhibits approximately 14% higher hardness than the alloy produced with 3 h of milling.
